overview: I4203 ties degraded-heading recovery, emergency field selection, and fuel accountability into one decision loop. The event standard is to use ATC to reduce heading workload when needed, keep a suitable recovery field in mind before the emergency, and compare planned fuel to actual fuel early enough that fuel never becomes a surprise.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: A no-gyro approach is available under radar control when directional gyro or stabilized compass information is inoperative, inaccurate, or no longer trusted.

children.text: Tell ATC the heading system is unreliable and request a no-gyro PAR, ASR, PAR W/O GS, or vectors to a visual approach if VMC supports it.
Comply with the normal PAR, ASR, or PAR W/O GS procedure; no-gyro only changes how ATC commands turns.
Configuration, minimums, lost-communication, missed-approach, and climbout discipline still come from the underlying approach.
ATC may initiate no-gyro vectors if the controller sees incorrect directional responses or suspects the pilot has lost directional awareness.
Before final, start the turn immediately when told 'turn left' or 'turn right' and use standard rate, not more than 30 degrees AOB, unless directed otherwise.
Stop the turn immediately when told 'stop turn.'
On final, use half-standard-rate turns unless the controller directs another rate.
Acknowledge instructions until ATC says no further acknowledgements are required.
Common errors are slow compliance, wrong turn rate, late before-approach configuration, poor DA/MDA transition, and mixing up missed approach, climbout, and lost-communication instructions.

items.text: Emergency field selection is a continuous habit: every OPS Check should update the nearest suitable recovery option based on fuel, engine/system state, weather, terrain, lighting, and airspace.

children.text: Preflight chart study should identify diverts along the route, not just at the destination. Note runway length, orientation, elevation, lighting, surface, approaches, and communications.
Local SOPs may set specific runway-size, surface, lighting, solo, or night requirements. Verify current local standards instead of relying on memory.
Use the FMS NRST page, charts, NAVAIDs, ATC, and visual references together; no single tool decides suitability by itself.
For a precautionary emergency landing, communicate if able without delaying the emergency procedure. The useful call is who you are, where you are, and what you need.
If an engine fails at night at or above 2000 feet AGL and a lighted runway is not immediately available, ejection is highly recommended if restart is not attempted or is unsuccessful.
If an engine fails below 2000 feet AGL, attempting a restart is not recommended; if a lighted runway is not immediately available, first priority is setting up to eject.

In a low-level engine malfunction, climb to cope. Airfields within an arc circumscribed by the wingtips may be reachable with an immediate turn and climb, but a suitable field much beyond about 3 NM is unlikely from low level.
A zoom from about 240 knots groundspeed can gain roughly 1300 feet; consider whether that altitude buys restart, field selection, or ejection margin.
Route abort triggers include insufficient fuel, aircraft malfunction, bird hazard, and weather.
In VMC, maintain terrain clearance and VFR altitude rules if possible, set the appropriate transponder code, maintain VMC, and coordinate with the controlling agency.
An abort into IMC is an emergency: climb immediately to at least ERAA, squawk 7700, contact ATC, and do not let route-finding distract from aircraft control.
If communications cannot be established at an unfamiliar field, observe traffic, runway markings, segmented circle, wind indicators, and pattern direction from a safe altitude if time permits.

items.text: Fuel management compares the fuel plan to the aircraft reality before a low-fuel decision is forced. The basic cockpit comparison is Estimated Fuel Remaining versus Actual Fuel Remaining.

children.text: During planning, calculate EFR by verifying actual fuel load, subtracting start/taxi/takeoff fuel, then subtracting each leg's estimated fuel burn.
At the end of each leg, compare AFR to EFR. AFR greater than or equal to EFR supports the plan; AFR less than EFR requires immediate investigation.
Likely causes include less fuel onboard at takeoff, higher climb or cruise fuel flow, slower groundspeed, math or flight-log error, unplanned routing, or fuel leak.
Make the comparison part of the OPS Check so the decision happens while there are still route, altitude, divert, and ATC options.
CNAF fuel planning requires sufficient usable fuel for meteorological factors and mission requirements.

If no alternate is required, plan fuel from takeoff to destination plus a 10% reserve. If an alternate is required, plan takeoff to the destination approach fix, then to the alternate, plus a 10% reserve.
The planned reserve after final landing may not be less than 20 minutes of flight; for turbine fixed-wing aircraft, compute that at maximum endurance at 10,000 feet.
The workbook uses the T-6B NATOPS/PCL maximum-endurance value of 333 PPH at 10,000 feet on a standard day, yielding about 111 pounds for 20 minutes and a rounded planning reserve of 115 pounds.
Local training minimums may be higher than the regulatory planning reserve; confirm current squadron/CNATRA minimum fuel and emergency fuel numbers before relying on them.
When fuel endurance becomes the controlling factor, use NATOPS maximum-endurance data instead of inventing a low-burn technique.
Maximum endurance AOA is 8.8 units; maximum range AOA is 4.4 units.
Recommended clean holding speed is 125 to 150 KIAS, but no slower than maximum endurance speed of 125 KIAS.
Use DRAFT for a divert request: destination, route, altitude, fuel remaining in hours plus minutes, and time en route.

Minimum fuel tells ATC no undue delay can be accepted; it is not itself an emergency. If traffic priority is needed to ensure a safe landing, declare emergency fuel and report fuel remaining in minutes.

studyNotes.summary: Use no-gyro vectors to reduce heading-reference workload, keep emergency recovery fields updated before the problem, and compare EFR to AFR early enough to protect divert options.

summary: No-gyro approach execution, emergency recovery-field selection, and fuel-management decision points.
title: No-Gyro and Fuel Management
